<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README, this project is an Electron‐based application called Responsively App—a browser that assists web developers with responsive design testing. In addition to the main desktop application, the repository also contains a browser extension and a “desktop-app-legacy” folder with older code. Here’s how to draw the best, detailed system design diagram for this project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Desktop Application (Modern)
     - Main Process: Located in the modern “desktop-app” directory (files under src/main such as main.ts, preload.ts, protocol-handler, app-updater, etc.). This manages the application lifecycle, native integrations, and communication channels.
     - Renderer Process: Found in the “desktop-app/src/renderer” directory. It contains the UI built with React/TypeScript. Also note the rich folder structure with components, context providers (e.g., ThemeProvider), and Redux-like store management (store folder).
     - Preload Scripts: Bridge the gap between the Main and Renderer processes and provide secure IPC channels.
     - Services & Utilities: The code under “src/main/…” and “src/renderer/lib” and “src/store” indicate custom services (e.g., screenshot service, permissions management) and utility functions.
   • Desktop Application – Legacy
     - The “desktop-app-legacy” directory contains an older version of the desktop application. This segment should be drawn as a separate block, perhaps noting that it uses a different configuration (older webpack configurations, JS rather than TS, different styling) but still represents the same overall functionality.
   • Browser Extension
     - Under the “browser-extension” folder, include the manifest, background scripts, and popup UI. This extension communicates with the desktop app (likely through local messaging or custom protocols) to pass URL links or commands for instant previews.

2. Show Relationships & Interactions:
   • Draw communication channels (using directional arrows) between the Main Process and Renderer Process via IPC. Denote where the preload scripts assist in this data exchange.
   • Show how the Browser Extension connects with the Desktop App. For example, indicate that when a user clicks on a link in the extension popup (background.js/popup.js), a message or protocol is sent to the Desktop App to open a new preview.
   • Optionally, you can add an “external clients” node (i.e., external services or device emulation profiles) that the app manages or mirrors user interactions across; this is suggested by the README feature of “mirrored user-interactions.”

3. Architectural Patterns & Design Principles:
   • Emphasize the Electron multi-process architecture – clearly separate Main and Renderer. Label these with “Electron main process” and “Electron renderer process” respectively.
   • Note the use of modular design: For example, the “desktop-app/src/renderer/components” folder is split into many individual React components, which can be grouped (e.g., navigation, previewers, toolbar, dialogs).
   • Mention that the architecture promotes separation of concerns – UI presentation (renderer), OS-level operations (main), and communication patterns via IPC.
   • Include build and configuration components such as webpack configurations (found in .erb and configs directories) to hint at bundling and type-checking with TypeScript.

4. Relevant Technologies & Frameworks:
   • Electron for desktop app functionalities.
   • React and Redux (or similar state management) for rendering and state handling.
   • Webpack (with multiple config files) for module bundling.
   • TypeScript – especially noted in the modern “desktop-app” directory.
   • Legacy JavaScript in “desktop-app-legacy.”
   • Node.js packages used in the browser extension (referenced in package.json) and in the build scripts.
   
5. Guidelines for Creating the Diagram:
   • Create separate blocks/boxes for each main component:
       - A “Desktop App (Modern)” box subdivided into “Main Process,” “Renderer Process,” and “Preload/Services.”
       - A “Desktop App – Legacy” box that shows a parallel architecture (even if it is less modular now, it can be annotated as a legacy alternative).
       - A “Browser Extension” box that includes its background script and UI components.
   • Use directional arrows to depict IPC, UI events, and data flows:
       - Show arrows from the Main Process to Renderer (for UI updates).
       - A separate bidirectional arrow between the Extension and Desktop App to represent message passing.
   • Use different colors or shapes to distinguish between different layers/type of components:
       - For instance, color-code “Electron core components,” “UI components,” “services/utilities,” and “external integrations.”
   • Clearly label each component with its role (e.g., “Electron Main: handles app lifecycle & native functions”, “React Renderer: displays responsive previews”, “Extension: sends URL commands to the app”).
   • Indicate technologies or configuration files at key intersections. For example, note “webpack.config.js” in the build pipeline or “tsconfig.json” near the TypeScript components.

6. Emphasize Details without Overcomplicating:
   • Capture all essential architectural elements. Even if the file tree might suggest many sub-folders, focus on high-level nodes and their internal subdivisions. 
   • Leverage boxes to “group” similar functionalities (e.g., grouping all Redux-related store files under a “State Management” banner).
   • Ensure that data flow directions (e.g., from the extension to the main process, and main to renderer) are clear.
   • Optionally annotate certain interactions (e.g., IPC communication, browser messaging) for clarity.

Using these guidelines, the principal software engineer should create a system design diagram that accurately represents every main facet of the project—from the modern Electron setup down to the browser extension and legacy code—thereby providing a comprehensive overview of how Responsively App is architected.

Remember to include:
   – Clear labels for every component.
   – Directional arrows denoting data flow and communication channels.
   – Consistent use of color coding or shapes to differentiate component types.
   – Annotations regarding used technologies (Electron, React, TypeScript, webpack) and design patterns (separation of concerns, modular architecture).

This detailed and structured diagram will serve as an excellent visual representation of the project’s architecture tailored specifically to Responsively App’s structure and purpose.
</explanation>
